title: Mina and the Wobbly Knots
markdown:
Mina the squirrel, her tail a big cinnamon-coloured fluff, was having a very wiggly day. Not her tail. That was as steady and impressive as ever. It was the knots. In the library cupboard.

The library was no ordinary library. Books seemed to whisper secrets. The air felt full of stories. A grand old building, smelling faintly of old paper, polish, and the occasional forgotten biscuit crumb. And it had a cupboard, perfectly ordinary-looking, tucked behind the Fabulous Fiction for Future Food Critics shelf, right next to a bunch of jam-making books. Inside were strings. Lots of strings. Knotted strings. And they were being dreadfully disobedient.

“Oh, bother and fuzz,” chattered Mina, peering in, whiskers twitching. She was supposed to be organising the lost buttons and stray bookmarks, a job that needed her tiny nimble paws to be careful. Today the strings were playing hopscotch with logic. One minute a knot sat smugly near the top of a faded blue string, and the next, poof, it had wiggled to the very bottom, looking quite pleased with itself. Another knot, holding a perfectly sensible position mid-string on a cheerful yellow cord, suddenly stretched itself impossibly long, like a sleepy cat reaching for a sunbeam.

“It’s an outrage,” Mina declared to a dust bunny that looked remarkably like a tiny fluffy sheep. She nudged it with her nose. “Knots are supposed to stay put. They have a job to do. They’re not supposed to wander like a flock of escaped sheep.”

Perched on the high parapet of the library tower was Tolliver. Tolliver was a gargoyle, excellent at observing, with eyes like smooth pebbles carved deep as if they held old secrets, and he always looked a bit grumpy. He’d been watching Mina’s frantic scurrying for days, the little flicker of cinnamon fur against the stone.

“What’s all the fuss, little nut-hoarder?” Tolliver rumbled, a sound like pebbles rolling down a hill. “Are the bookmarks planning a rebellion? Have the buttons declared they want to be free?”

Mina scrambled up the ivy-covered wall, claws gripping rough stone and thick green leaves. She reached Tolliver’s perch, heart beating fast from the climb. “It’s the strings, Tolliver. The ones in the old cupboard. They’re acting like slippery eels in a soup pot.”

Tolliver blinked slowly, which for a gargoyle was quite an effort. “Strings do what they do, Mina. They tangle. They knot. They get lost. Last week I saw a pigeon try to build a nest out of a library card. Now that was a crisis.” He punctuated this with a low stone chuckle.

Mina insisted, bright eyes wide. “They’re changing. It’s not just tangling. It’s like they’re alive. Look.” She dashed back to the cupboard, tail giving an indignant flick, and pulled out a particularly long faded blue string. Three neat knots, spaced like pearls. “See? Three knots. Perfectly sensible. Now watch.” She turned away for a single second to look at a shiny spiderweb. When she turned back, the blue string had four knots, and the original three had inched closer together, as if whispering secrets. “Four knots. And they’ve all shifted.”

Tolliver grumbled, rocks falling far away. “Probably a draft. Or a particularly funny bookworm. Perhaps it’s been reading too many adventure stories and decided to liven things up.”

Mina sighed like tiny wind chimes. She tied the strings with extra-strong squirrel knots. They untied themselves overnight. She tried to smooth them out. They immediately tied themselves into new, even more baffling knots, some looking a lot like tiny tangled hedgehogs. The librarian, Mrs. Glimmer, whose glasses always slid down her nose, simply patted Mina’s head. “Oh, those old cupboard strings, dear. Always up to something. Probably just playing amongst themselves when no one’s looking.” Mina knew it was more. It was a puzzle, magnificent, infuriating, tantalizing, and Mina adored puzzles.

Days turned into a week. Mina spent her afternoons with her nose practically glued to the strings, a little satchel of carefully chosen nuts to sustain her, nibbling thoughtfully. Tolliver watched from his high spot, a little amused and a little worried. He could see the frustration in her bright eyes, and her tail drooped when a knot wouldn’t give up its secrets.

One afternoon, slumped against the cupboard door, utterly defeated, her gaze fell on a book lying open on a nearby table. An old crumbly book with faded gold letters: Lost Civilizations and Their Clever Tricks. A picture of coloured strings and knots, arranged in a special planned way.

“Wait a minute,” Mina whispered, whiskers twitching so fast they looked like a blurry halo. She remembered a lunchtime talk by a historian about the ancient Inca people. They had used knots to count. To keep records. She’d thought it sounded like a tricky way to count.

Her heart did a little somersault. She scrambled to the book, claws soft on the polished floor, and looked closely. The strings in the picture looked remarkably like the ones in the cupboard. The arrangement of knots, the different colours… it was starting to click, like the parts of a very complicated old lock.

“Tolliver,” she squeaked, so loud a nearby shelf of encyclopedias shook. “These aren’t just wobbly strings. They’re quipu.”

Tolliver, who had been half-dozing, perked up. “Quipu? Sounds like something a grumpy goose might say before breakfast. Or maybe a rude badger.”

“No. It’s an ancient Inca counting system. They used knots to record numbers and information. The position of the knot, how many there are, the colour of the string, the type of knot itself. It all means something.” Mina’s tiny paws vibrated. She dashed back to the cupboard, mind buzzing like a busy bee.

She grabbed the faded blue string, the one that had started with three knots. She counted carefully. “Four. What could four mean?” The red string had two knots. The yellow one, five. She looked at the diagrams, nose almost touching the page. The way the knots were placed, the kind of knot itself, wasn’t random. It was a code. A smart, complicated, old code.

With growing excitement, chattering to herself, Mina began to decipher. The blue string with four knots, compared to the book’s examples, showed how many times the library’s big old clock had chimed that week. The red string with two knots: the number of new books that had arrived. The yellow one with five: the number of times Mrs. Glimmer had made her special lavender tea.

The cupboard wasn’t just a cupboard. It was a secret history record, a fun collection of the library’s daily life, kept meticulously by the librarian who had left, who had loved old ways of counting. The strings weren’t changing randomly. They were being gently nudged by the vibrations of the clock tower, the old building creaking, and even Mrs. Glimmer stamping new books. A living history book, made of string.

Mrs. Glimmer was very happy when Mina explained. Her spectacles slid all the way down her nose, and she let out a happy gasp. She declared the cupboard the Library’s Whispering History Chest and told everyone about Mina’s clever discovery. The children who visited liked looking at the strings and guessing what they meant, with Mina often there to explain, tail flicking extra happily over a particularly complex knot. Tolliver admitted, in his gruff way, that perhaps some strings were useful, not just for tangling. He even let a small stony smile appear. From his high perch he kept watching over the Whispering History Chest, the town’s most wonderfully wobbly, knotty, and delightful secret.
